items.title: Darius Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 29, 2024
items.q: Iola’s — the short version of what she said, what she’s also said about herself is she’s intolerant of intolerance. And you know I think in the family we’re all like that.

ctx.x: Okay. I wanted to offer up a couple of quotes. And this one comes from Iola. Near the end of my interview with her I said, “What makes you angry?” And she paused for a moment and then she said, “Injustice — it’s not a just world. I hate to see anyone treated badly, not even the right to be themselves and the stereotyping of people. That I really can’t tolerate. That’s where I’m intolerant.” It looks to me like you inherited some of that.

Yeah. Well everyone — I think everyone grows up thinking they learn the difference between right and wrong from their parents and yet we can have disagreements within our societies so we don’t all learn the same things. But yeah, Iola’s — the short version of what she said, what she’s also said about herself is she’s intolerant of intolerance. And you know I think in the family we’re all like that. We’ve all, to one degree or another,

been involved with the Civil Rights Movement or, more overtly I’ve been in the political system — cultural/political struggle in South Africa. But it’s not literally inherited. My wife Cathy is just the same. You know she was an activist when it was very dangerous to be one. You know once she was with me the worst thing they could do is kick us out of the country. But when she was a university student and national secretary of the Progressive Party and dealing with the, you know very heavy handed government…

items.title: Iola Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, CT, July 17, 2011
items.q: I know I’ve heard our oldest one, Darius, explain

ctx.x: Matthew said when asked about making a living as a musician he said, “I didn’t know there was any other way.”

I know. I think that’s the way all of them felt, that music was just around them all the time when they were growing up, and I know I’ve heard our oldest one, Darius, explain, it just seemed like the grown-ups were having so much fun and they were just playing and it just seemed like something that, “That’s what I want to do when I grow up.” And they all started taking lessons when they were pretty young and they drifted from one instrument to another and finally settled on what they wanted to play. And they’re…
Did they have a sense early on that their — I’m not sure how to ask this — that their father was a well-known public figure? Did they understand that?
